Meeting: Quantaflow pilot econ sync & caching debrief
Date/Time: 2026-05-15 16:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Diego Ramos (Redwood AE), Lena Park (Redwood SE), Omar Velasquez (Redwood CSM); Maya Singh (CTO), Tom Ruiz (ML Eng), Priya Nair (Product), Ethan Cole (Infra)

Auto-summary: (auto) Briefly: caching shows ~35-55% token cost reduction on long-context chat; batching improves tokens/sec but can add 40-120ms tail latency depending on traffic shape.

[00:00:03] Diego Ramos: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — is this the same group from last week?
[00:00:08] Maya Singh: Yep, Maya here. Got the devs and Tom is on for perf bits.
[00:00:12] Tom Ruiz: morning afternoon, yeah.
[00:00:14] Diego Ramos: Cool. High level agenda — we wanted to walk through the econ numbers from the last 72 hour run, talk about caching/ batching adjustments, and decide on the A/B and next benchmark. Lena, I'll pass to you for the numbers.
[00:00:26] Lena Park: Great. So we pulled the metrics from your dev cluster between Tuesday 10am and Thursday 10am. Baseline used rdlm-13b-std (not quantized), prefix cache disabled, batching policy: conservative (max batch size 8, 60ms wait). Observed avg tokens/sec per GPU ~ 220, tokens per dollar approx 12k tokens/$ for generation workloads.
[00:00:46] Speaker 2: (mumble) the tokens per dollar seems...
[00:00:50] Lena Park: Right, with no caching that's expected. After enabling prefix KV caching for the chat flows we saw tokens/sec stay similar but effective tokens per dollar increased to 18k tokens/$ — about 50% improvement for long-horizon sessions where there's repeated context reuse. In the hybrid run where we allowed larger batches (max 24, 20ms wait) we saw tokens/sec jump to 390 but p95 latency increased from 210ms to 320ms for small-ish requests.
[00:01:21] Tom Ruiz: When you say long-horizon, what's the median session length? Ours is about 700 tokens average but tails go to 4k when users paste docs.
[00:01:30] Lena Park: median ~650, tail 3k-4k — that's exactly where prefix cache helps the most. But I want to call out that for the paste-heavy flows batching contributed less to cost reduction because KV cache already avoided re-computation for the prefix tokens.
[00:01:44] Priya Nair: So caching is always win then? Why not enable everywhere?
[00:01:48] Lena Park: Mostly yes for chat-like flows, but three caveats: 1) cache size & eviction — your dev cluster footprint has 12GB per replica for KV; if we enable widely you'll need more memory or frequent misses; 2) data residency / PII — if you have ephemeral private data, need controls for TTL and anonymization; 3) correctness — some prompts are sensitive to state so you might want selective cache invalidation.
[00:02:15] Ethan Cole: On the infra side, memory is the main constraint. We saw a few OOMs when we tested with cache enabled + big batches. Could be tuning, but it's a concern.
[00:02:24] Lena Park: Yeah, those OOMs were on the rdlm-13b-std instances with the default KV page size. We recommended smaller page sizes and a conservative LRU eviction for now. Also quantization reduces memory pressure — 4-bit quant reduced memory footprint ~28% in our runs but added a small delta in quality for code generation prompts.
[00:02:42] Maya Singh: How did quality look? Our product team is real sensitive to hallucination spikes, especially on internal doc synthesis.
[00:02:48] Lena Park: For the sequestered eval sets we ran, 4-bit int8-ish quant (the team used int4 per-layer mixed) had negligible delta on general chat but for code/document synthesis we saw a 1.5-2% drop in exact-match metrics. We can isolate quantized variants for lower-cost endpoints and keep a full precision path for critical flows.
[00:03:10] Diego Ramos: Quick commercial point — given those deltas, the tokens/sec/$ vs quality tradeoff maps to different pricing tiers. But focusing on the POC, I want a clear plan: what is the pillar that gives you biggest unit-cost wins without hurting UX?
[00:03:21] Tom Ruiz: Sounds like prefix KV caching + targeted quantization where we can accept slight quality loss. Then use batching only in non-interactive flows.
[00:03:29] Lena Park: Exactly. Also the routing policy — for read-heavy retrieval flows we suggest a cold path that hits a cheaper quantized model and a hot path that keeps full precision with prefix caching. That reduces overall spend and preserves quality on the important queries.
[00:03:42] Maya Singh: Can you give ballpark numbers for net savings if we adopt that hybrid?
[00:03:46] Lena Park: On your workload mix we estimate 40-55% reduction in tokens cost for chat-dominant sessions, and 20-30% for mixed flows. Batch-only changes gave another 10-20% for throughput-focused endpoints but increased tail latency so UX tradeoffs apply.
[00:04:03] Priya Nair: There's also the question of dedicated capacity. If we go dedicated, does that change these numbers?
[00:04:09] Lena Park: Dedicated helps with predictable throughput and occasional lower unit costs because of reserved capacity. In dedicated runs, tokens/sec per GPU was about 5-8% better due to kernel selection and fewer multi-tenant perturbations. But the big wins still come from caching.
[00:04:23] Diego Ramos: Omar, anything from your CS side about adoption blockers?
[00:04:26] Omar Velasquez: Just adding — logging and observability are critical. We need tracing around cache hits/misses, batch sizes, and per-request cost. We recommended adding a cost header per response to help product owners.
[00:04:38] Ethan Cole: We tried the header earlier but our pipeline didn't ingest it cleanly. We'll fix. Also, question: you mentioned TTL and anonymization for caching — how granular is that control?
[00:04:47] Lena Park: You can set per-route TTLs, enable redaction hooks before caching, and opt-out via request flag. We'll send the runbook for implementing those hooks.
[00:04:56] Speaker 3: (faint) right right
[00:05:00] Tom Ruiz: On the A/B you proposed, how do you want to split traffic and for how long to get statistical confidence? Our daily volume is ~120k requests.
[00:05:09] Lena Park: For a clear signal on tokens/dollar and latency, a 50/50 split for 48-72 hours should be sufficient. We'll track cost per session, p95 latency, and failed requests. Also capture distribution of session lengths because effectiveness of caching is correlated.
[00:05:26] Diego Ramos: We'll provide a spreadsheet with the metrics to compute tokens per dollar — did you get a chance to look at the initial one?
[00:05:31] Maya Singh: Saw it briefly, we had some questions on the assumptions for GPU pricing.
[00:05:35] Diego Ramos: Yeah we used your public cloud rates for the dev cluster plus a Redwood overhead estimate — it's in the notes; we'll tighten it after you share exact cloud SKUs.
[00:05:43] Priya Nair: One operational concern — when KV cache evicts entries during peak, do we expect latency spikes?
[00:05:49] Lena Park: Eviction itself shouldn't spike latency; the spike is generally due to cache miss causing recompute of the whole prefix. To mitigate that we pre-warm caches for expected hot sessions and also do progressive invalidation.
[00:06:02] Maya Singh: Any safety/regulatory issues if we keep caches for 24 hours? We have some regulated customer data.
[00:06:07] Diego Ramos: We recommend shorter TTLs for regulated flows and full encryption at rest for cache shards. Also KMS integration is available; we'll include that in the security doc.
[00:06:16] Ethan Cole: Great — send us the KMS integration notes.
[00:06:19] Lena Park: Will do.
[00:06:21] Tom Ruiz: Switching gears — batching tuning: you suggested hybrid dynamic batching where small low-latency requests get priority, and larger requests are batched more aggressively. How complex is that to implement?
[00:06:31] Lena Park: It's an out-of-the-box policy in Redwood runtime — you tag routes with latency tiers. The runtime then uses an exponential backoff and target batch size per tier. We'll push the sample config for your routes.
[00:06:44] Priya Nair: Can the routing also fallback automatically to a cheaper model if capacity is constrained?
[00:06:48] Diego Ramos: Yes, that's the fallback policy. You can configure a cheaper variant for best-effort traffic and keep premium traffic pinned. We'll send a recommended policy.
[00:06:56] Maya Singh: One more thing — our product team noticed a small but consistent drift in output style after quantization. Is there a way to quickly validate quality in CI?
[00:07:04] Lena Park: Yes, Redwood Optimize has eval hooks and you can run a prompt-set regression daily. We can set up a quality gate that fails deployment if rouge/EM drops beyond threshold.
[00:07:15] Diego Ramos: Ok let's recap. Action items: Redwood to send tuned batching + caching spreadsheet and runbook; Quantaflow to run 48-72h A/B on KV cache with 50/50 split; Quantaflow to enable tracing and share logs; schedule dedicated capacity benchmark next Wed if initial A/B looks good. Any objections?
[00:07:33] Maya Singh: No objections. One ask — bring one of your SREs to the dedicated benchmark so we can pair on tuning.
[00:07:39] Omar Velasquez: Sure, we'll have Lena and one SRE from Redwood in the benchmark session.
[00:07:44] Tom Ruiz: Quick nit — can you add a sample curl that shows cache-control headers so we can test locally?
[00:07:50] Lena Park: Yep, we'll include that and a terraform snippet for runtime flags.
[00:07:55] Priya Nair: Great. I'm also going to add product acceptance criteria — no worse than 5% latency regression for interactive flows.
[00:08:03] Diego Ramos: Noted. Any final questions?
[00:08:06] Ethan Cole: Nothing here.
[00:08:08] Maya Singh: All good. Thanks all.
[00:08:11] Diego Ramos: Thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts.

(Transcript notes: occasional word recognition errors near 00:00:46 and 00:04:56; speaker labels auto-assigned in a couple of spots.)

End of meeting.
